title: Employment Insurance
subtitle: Turn a sudden work interruption into an organized claim

blocks.text: Losing a job already rearranges the week. EI then asks for dates, hours and passwords precisely when the brain has decided to store only the lyrics to a 2009 commercial.

Employment Insurance gives you short-term income when you stop earning in certain ways. Regular benefits are for people who lose insured work through no fault of their own and stay ready, willing and able to work while they look for a suitable job. Other EI benefits cover sickness, a new baby, parenting and caring for someone who is ill.
Apply as soon as work stops, even if your Record of Employment has not arrived. If you wait more than four weeks after your last day of work, you may lose benefits.

items.title: “EI is automatic because premiums appeared on my paycheque.”
items.text: Premiums pay for the insurance. They do not decide your claim. You must apply and meet the rules for the benefit you need. Pay stubs are not tiny approval letters.

blocks.text: Service Canada: Employment Insurance
Applying the right way in your first week protects benefits you have already paid for.
blocks.detail: The reason you stopped working, your hours and your weekly reports decide whether the money arrives.
blocks.extra: Section 02 starts with the reason work stopped.

sections.title: Start With the Reason Work Stopped

items.title: A BREAK IN WORK
items.text: For regular EI, you usually need insured work and at least seven days in a row with no work and no pay.

items.title: WHY THE JOB ENDED
items.text: Losing your job through no fault of your own is the usual route. Quitting, misconduct, a strike, school or travel can mean a closer look.

items.title: HOURS FOR YOUR REGION
items.text: You normally need 420 to 700 insured hours, based on the jobless rate in your EI region.

items.title: STAYING AVAILABLE
items.text: Regular EI needs you to be ready, willing and able to work, with a written record of your job search.

blocks.text: The hours usually count from the past 52 weeks, or from when your last claim began if that is shorter.
Your EI region depends on where you live, which may not be where you worked. Use the official postal code lookup for the date your claim starts.
Regular EI needs you to be available and to keep a record of your job search. Sickness EI uses a different test: you would be available to work if not for your health condition.

items.title: “Every job loss qualifies for regular EI as long as enough hours were worked.”
items.text: Why the job ended, the break in pay, being available and looking for work all matter too. Hours are one gate, not the entire airport.

blocks.text: Service Canada: EI eligibility

sections.title: The Application Opens Your File. Reports Keep It Moving.

blocks.text: Apply online with your work dates, employer details, why the job ended, bank details and the ID details asked for. Employers may send your Record of Employment online or give you a paper copy. List every employer. Service Canada decides which pay and hours count.
In 2026, the basic rate is usually 55% of your average insured weekly pay, up to $729 a week. Regular benefits may last 14 to 45 weeks, depending on the jobless rate in your region and your hours.

After you apply, send your report every two weeks, on time and accurate. List any work, hours, pay before tax, whether you were available, training, travel and other money they ask about. Keep a job-search log with employers, dates, how you applied, the job and what happened.

If you work while on a regular claim, EI usually drops by 50 cents for each dollar you earn, until your pay reaches 90% of the weekly amount used to set up your claim. Above that, EI drops dollar for dollar.

items.title: “Part-time earnings can be omitted because EI will find them later.”
items.text: You must report all work and pay for the week you earned it. Letting the data matching find it later is an expensive paperwork hobby.

blocks.text: Key takeaway
Apply right away, use the right EI route and keep a record every week. The rules still apply after you are approved, so report your availability, work, pay and changes accurately.

sections.title: Dylan and the Record That Was Still Commuting

blocks.text: Meet Dylan
paragraphs: Dylan Fraser loses his job at a car parts plant in Windsor. His goal is to keep up with rent and his truck payment until he finds new work. His boss says the Record of Employment will arrive soon. Dylan decides to wait for it before he applies.
Two weeks pass. The record seems to be commuting from another province by canoe. Then a friend mentions the four-week rule. If Dylan waits too long, he could lose benefits.
That same week, a neighbour pays him $160 cash for a day of landscaping. Dylan figures a small amount like that is too polite to mention.

He has two choices to make. He can keep waiting for the record, or apply now without it. And he can leave out the $160, or report it. Dylan applies that night and notes that his record is missing. On his first report, he lists the landscaping day and the $160 for the week he earned it.
He also looks up his region’s hours and starts a job-search log: where he applied, when and what happened.

The twist comes a week later. The record finally arrives, with the wrong last day of work. Because Dylan had already applied, he only has to send the fix, not start over. He calls his old employer, and they send a corrected copy.
Service Canada decides the claim. Dylan could not control the record’s travel speed. He did control his application date, his weekly reports and his honesty about the $160.

blocks.text: A late or wrong Record of Employment is something to follow up on, not a reason to put off applying. Note when you contacted your employer and tell Service Canada what is missing.
Dylan protected his claim by applying before the paperwork arrived and reporting every dollar he earned.
blocks.detail: Applying early and reporting honestly keeps your claim safe even when your employer is slow.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: What belongs in a check for regular EI?
items.detail: Insured work, the reason work stopped, a break in pay, enough hours for your region, being available and an active job search.

items.title: Why can two workers need a different number of hours?
items.detail: It depends on the jobless rate in each person’s EI region and the date their claim starts.

items.title: Should you wait for your Record of Employment before you apply?
items.detail: No. Apply as soon as work stops, and follow up on a missing or wrong record separately.

items.title: What goes in your report every two weeks?
items.detail: Work, hours, pay before tax, whether you were available, training, travel and any other money they ask about for those weeks.

items.title: How does working while on a claim usually affect EI?
items.detail: EI usually drops by 50 cents for each dollar you earn until your pay reaches 90% of the weekly amount used to set up your claim. Above that, it drops dollar for dollar.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): EI Claim Launch and Weekly Reporting Log

blocks.text: Keep claim codes, your SIN and bank details out of this form. Store official logins and papers somewhere safe.
For first EI claims that start from March 30, 2025 to October 10, 2026, the usual one-week waiting period is waived for now. Report what happened in the week it happened, even if the pay comes later.

items.title: EI
items.text: Employment Insurance. Short-term income when you stop working in certain ways.

items.title: Insurable employment
items.text: Work covered by EI premiums and EI rules.

items.title: ROE
items.text: Record of Employment. It shows your work and why it stopped.

items.title: Qualifying period
items.text: The time used to count your insured hours.

items.title: EI economic region
items.text: The local job-market area that sets the hours and weeks you need.

items.title: Waiting period
items.text: Usually an unpaid first week. It is waived for now for some claims.

items.title: Biweekly report
items.text: The report you send every two weeks to keep getting paid.

quiz.question: True or False: “EI is automatic because premiums appeared on my paycheque.”

questions: What was your last day of work, and have you applied yet? (Applied / Not yet / Not sure)
Why did your job end? (Laid off / Quit / Fired / Sick / New baby or caregiving / Not sure)
Has your Record of Employment arrived, and is it correct? (Yes / Not yet / It has a mistake / Not sure)
About how many hours did you work in the past year? An estimate is fine.
Have you done any paid work since you stopped? List the week and the amount. Write “none” if not.
Where will you keep your job-search log, and when is your next report due?
samples: Not yet. My employer says next week.
One day of landscaping in the week of October 12, $160.
A notebook in my truck. My next report is due October 20.
